item.description:
**A folder from a host arrived without its empty folders.** Dragging a folder from a host onto this Mac carried every file in it, but none of the folders that held nothing — and dragging an empty folder brought nothing across at all, while the transfer said it had finished. Every folder arrives now, empty or not, and a folder sent up and brought back is the folder it was.
**A host-key question in a narrow window could go unasked.** With large text, or a window narrow enough, ssh's question about a new machine's key wraps across several lines of the terminal. Past two of them it was not seen, so ssh sat waiting for an answer the app never asked you for. It is asked now however many lines it takes, and the dialog shows the whole question, fingerprint included.
**Answering a host-key question could bring it back for an instant.** In the moment between your answer and the terminal showing it, the question could reappear — and a click in that moment typed into the shell. An answered question stays answered.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 448 checks to 459, and folders are now among what it carries for real against OpenSSH's own server: the first fix above was found the first time anything tested a folder at all.

**Accepting a new host key could bring the question straight back.** The first time you connect to a machine, ssh asks whether to trust its key. On a server that logs in quietly — no "last login" line, no message of the day — saying yes was not enough: the question came back at once, as though it had never been answered. Saying yes a second time then typed `yes` into the shell you had just logged into, which runs the `yes` command and fills the terminal with `y` until you press Control-C; saying no typed `no` into it instead. A question you have answered now stays answered.
**A terminal no longer carries the app's own connections with it.** When a terminal session started, the `ssh` behind it was handed copies of whatever the app had open at that moment — the connections behind an open SFTP window, and the watch the app keeps on your host list — and held them for as long as it ran. Nothing ever used them, but nothing should have been handed them either. They stay with the app now.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 421 checks to 448, and for the first time it holds the app against the real thing rather than a stand-in: SFTP against OpenSSH's own server, and `ssh` itself — connecting, keys, jump hosts, and a terminal answering a real host-key question — against a server started for the length of each test. The first fix above was found that way, on the first run of a test written to look.

**New Local Shell opened at the root of the disk.** A shell started here inherits the app's own working directory, and an app launched the ordinary way — from the Dock, from Finder — has `/`. So a local shell opened at the root of the disk rather than in your home directory, in every release up to 0.0.5. It opens at home now, and the test for it asks the shell itself where it started rather than reading the screen.
**A file pane could wait for ever.** Nothing in SFTP puts a limit on how long a reply may take, and the app had nothing of its own either: a request the far end never answered left a pane sitting on "Connecting…", or on a listing that was never going to arrive. Worse, it could not even be asked again — the guard that stops one pane opening twice was released at the end of the request, and a request that never ends never reaches it. A request now gives up after half a minute, says which kind of request went unanswered, and leaves the pane showing that rather than nothing.
**Closing the SFTP window left its connections running.** Letting go of the window released the window and the browser inside it, but not the `ssh` each pane was talking through, so one connection per connected pane stayed open until the app quit. Closing the window now ends them. If a question about replacing files was still on screen when it closed, that is answered too — Cancel, so nothing is carried on the way out — rather than leaving the copy behind it waiting on an answer nobody could give any more.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 403 checks to 421, and what is new in it is the file browser's own orchestration — the guard above, and the replace question driven against a copy genuinely parked on it — along with the SFTP deadline and the two ends of a connection that stops answering.
